reference_text:
Welcome to the course. We will work through each concept carefully, connect the
ideas step by step, and use practical examples to make technical topics easier
to understand. When we introduce a new method, focus first on the problem it
solves and why it is useful. For example, in machine learning, features are the
information we give the model, while the target is what we want it to predict.
Now consider a simple question: what changes when the data contains missing
values? We will think through the reason and then look at the code. In Python,
we can inspect the data, run one small step at a time, and explain what the
result means. The goal is to understand the logic, not simply memorize syntax.

slides.title: Dictionaries & Sets
slides.transcript:
Welcome to Module 5. Lists and tuples organize values by position. Dictionaries and sets give us two new ideas: labels and uniqueness.

A dictionary stores key-value pairs, so instead of remembering that a value is at position two, we can retrieve it by a meaningful label. A set automatically keeps unique values.

[tts-break]

These structures are extremely useful for records, category counts, lookup tables, unique IDs, and data-cleaning tasks.

slides.title: How to use this page
slides.transcript:
As you work through the examples, pay attention to how the data is being accessed.

With a dictionary, ask which key identifies the value. With a set, ask what duplicates disappear or what group comparison is being performed.

[tts-break]

Run the code, then change one key, one value, or one set item. Small experiments will make the behavior much easier to remember.

slides.title: Learning path for Module 5
slides.transcript:
We’ll begin with dictionary basics: creating labeled data, retrieving values, and updating records.

Then we’ll loop through keys and values, count categories, represent small datasets, and work with nested dictionaries.

After that, sets help us remove duplicates, compare groups, and test membership.

[tts-break]

The final examples combine dictionaries and sets in one analytics workflow.

slides.title: Why dictionaries and sets matter
slides.transcript:
Lists are great when position matters. Dictionaries are better when labels matter, and sets are useful when uniqueness matters.

With a list, scores zero means “the first value.” With a dictionary, student score lets the key itself describe the meaning.

A set is different again: it focuses on distinct values rather than position.

[tts-break]

In analytics, dictionaries often represent records or counts, while sets help with unique categories, IDs, and group comparisons.

slides.title: Create a dictionary
slides.transcript:
Let’s build a customer record as a dictionary.

The keys are id, visits, total_spent, and status. Each key points to one value. Instead of remembering positions, we can ask directly for customer id or customer visits.

[tts-break]

That makes the code much more readable. Customer bracket id clearly means “give me the customer ID.”

Try adding another key such as region or membership level and print it.

slides.title: Access values safely
slides.transcript:
There are two common ways to retrieve dictionary values.

Square brackets work when you are confident the key exists. Ticket priority is safe because priority is present in the record.

Get is useful when a key may be missing. Owner does not exist, so ticket dot get returns the default value “unassigned” instead of raising an error.

[tts-break]

This is especially helpful with real-world records where some fields may be optional or incomplete.

slides.title: Update a dictionary
slides.transcript:
Dictionaries are mutable, so a record can change over time.

Projects begins at two and is updated to three. Department is a completely new key, so assignment adds it. Pop removes role and returns the removed value.

[tts-break]

This mirrors many real data workflows: a record arrives, fields are corrected or enriched, and outdated fields may be removed.

Run the example and watch the record change step by step.

slides.title: Loop through a dictionary
slides.transcript:
A dictionary can be looped in several ways. Keys gives labels, values gives the stored values, and items gives both together.

Here items is the most useful because we want both the survey question and its score.

After printing each pair, the values are averaged. Four, five, and three have an average of four.

[tts-break]

This is a common pattern when the labels matter during reporting but the values are used for calculation.

slides.title: Count categories with a dictionary
slides.transcript:
Frequency counting is one of the most useful dictionary patterns.

We begin with an empty dictionary. For each channel, get looks for the current count. If the channel has not appeared yet, the default is zero. Then we add one.

[tts-break]

For the current list, web appears three times, email twice, and store once.

This initialize-and-increment pattern is the foundation of many category summaries.

slides.title: Represent records with dictionaries
slides.transcript:
A list of dictionaries looks very much like a small table.

Each dictionary is one order, and the keys act like column names: order_id, channel, and amount.

The loop processes one order at a time, adds its amount to the running total, and prints the record.

[tts-break]

The three amounts add to one hundred fifty-five dollars and seventy-five cents.

This structure is important because Pandas DataFrames are often created from records that look exactly like this.

slides.title: Nested dictionaries
slides.transcript:
A dictionary can contain another dictionary, which lets us organize related fields into sections.

The employee record contains basic information plus a skills dictionary. To reach the Python skill level, we first access skills and then access python inside that nested dictionary.

[tts-break]

Nested structures are common in JSON files and APIs, so learning to follow one key at a time is a useful practical skill.

slides.title: Create a set
slides.transcript:
A set keeps only unique values.

The channels list contains web three times and email twice. When we convert it to a set, the duplicates disappear and we are left with web, email, and store.

[tts-break]

Do not depend on a set for meaningful ordering. Its main purpose here is uniqueness.

Sets are useful when you need distinct categories, unique IDs, or a quick count of unique values.

slides.title: Set operations
slides.transcript:
Sets also make group comparison very convenient.

Union gives every customer who appeared in either season. Intersection gives customers in both seasons, which here are C103 and C104.

Spring minus summer gives customers who appeared only in spring, while summer minus spring gives those who appeared only in summer.

[tts-break]

These operations are useful for comparing cohorts, membership lists, categories, and other groups.

slides.title: Membership testing
slides.transcript:
The in operator asks whether a value belongs to a collection.

Allowed_statuses contains new, open, and closed. The loop checks each submitted status against that set.

New and closed are valid. Pending and review are not in the allowed set, so they are flagged for review.

[tts-break]

This pattern is useful for validation because sets make membership rules clear and efficient.

slides.title: Dictionary + set workflow
slides.transcript:
Now we combine the two structures in one order-processing example.

The dictionary totals_by_channel keeps a running sales total for each channel. The set unique_customers stores customer IDs without duplicates.

[tts-break]

C101 appears twice, but the set still counts that customer only once. The dictionary, however, adds both web orders to the web total.

This is a nice example of choosing a structure based on the question: dictionaries for labeled totals, sets for uniqueness.

slides.title: Choose the right structure
slides.transcript:
At this point we have four core collection types.

Use a list when order matters and duplicates are allowed. Use a tuple for a fixed record. Use a dictionary when values need meaningful labels. Use a set when you need uniqueness or group comparison.

[tts-break]

The goal is not to memorize a rigid rule. Ask how the data will be accessed and changed. That usually points you toward the right structure.

slides.title: Module 5 wrap-up
slides.transcript:
Let’s review what you can now do.

You can create dictionaries, retrieve values safely, update records, loop through key-value pairs, and build frequency counts. You can use sets to remove duplicates, compare groups, and validate membership.

[tts-break]

These structures give us more realistic ways to organize data in Python.

Next, we’ll use packages and object-oriented ideas to organize larger programs.

[tts-break]

In Module 6, we’ll focus on organizing larger Python programs. You’ll see how modules and packages help separate code into reusable files, and we’ll introduce object-oriented programming so related data and behavior can be organized together. This is an important step from small scripts toward maintainable applications.
